chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, altogether from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them), said:

I said to him, 'For the one who does not know whether he is in the fourth or in the two, and he has secured the two,' he said: 'He should bow in two rak'at and perform four prostrations while standing, with the Opening of the Book, and perform Tashahhud, and there is nothing upon him; and if he does not know whether he is in the three or in the four, and he has secured the three, he stands and adds another to them, and there is nothing upon him.'

And he does not invalidate certainty with doubt, nor does he insert doubt into certainty, nor does he mix one with the other, but rather he invalidates doubt with certainty and completes upon certainty, so he builds upon it, and he does not count the doubt in any of the states.

key_terms.فَاتِحَةِ الْكِتَابِ: The Opening of the Book (Surah Al-Fatiha)
key_terms.يَبْنِي عَلَيْهِ: Builds upon it (legal principle of relying on certainty)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for prayer when one is unsure whether they have completed two or three rak'at?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the foundational Shia principle of 'building upon certainty' (bina' ala al-yaqin), where doubt is dismissed rather than requiring the reconstruction of the prayer. It details specific procedural remedies, such as adding a rak'ah or performing sajdat al-shakk, ensuring the validity of the prayer despite uncertainty. This ruling reflects the juristic preference for preserving the established act over the potential defect introduced by doubt.
